items.prompt_md: What is the role of the 'unmark' step after the recursive call in grid backtracking?
options: It restores the cell so that other routes, including routes from other starting cells, can use it
It frees memory used by the recursion
It prevents the same route from being counted twice
It marks the cell as a dead end
items.answer: It restores the cell so that other routes, including routes from other starting cells, can use it
items.explanation_md: The marks should represent only the cells on the current route. Without the restore, a later route would see cells as used that are no longer on its path and the maximum would be missed.

items.prompt_md: How does this differ from the flood fill of an island-counting problem?
options: Flood fill uses BFS, backtracking uses DFS
In flood fill cells stay visited forever; in backtracking they are unmarked on return
Flood fill revisits cells, backtracking never does
There is no difference besides naming
items.answer: In flood fill cells stay visited forever; in backtracking they are unmarked on return
items.explanation_md: Flood fill wants each cell visited once overall. Backtracking wants every cell to be available to every route that does not already contain it. Both may use DFS.

items.prompt_md: A student writes the grid-gold DFS but forgets `grid[r][c] = gold` at the end. What happens?
options: Cells get permanently zeroed, so later starting cells see a shrunken grid and the answer can be too small
Nothing: the answer is still correct
items.answer: Cells get permanently zeroed, so later starting cells see a shrunken grid and the answer can be too small
items.explanation_md: Each zeroed cell becomes unavailable to every later route. The first start may still be right but later starts are compared against a corrupted grid. There is no infinite recursion because the marked cell prevents re-entry.

items.prompt_md: Why is a cell marked BEFORE exploring its neighbours rather than after?
options: To make the neighbour check faster
To count the cell's value only once at the end
Otherwise a neighbour could step straight back onto the current cell and the route would reuse it
items.answer: Otherwise a neighbour could step straight back onto the current cell and the route would reuse it
items.explanation_md: The mark is the O(1) 'already on this route' test. Marking after the loop would allow a two-cell ping-pong that never terminates.

items.prompt_md: Why can't a right/down-only DP solve the free-movement gold problem?
options: With four-direction movement and no revisits, the value depends on the whole set of cells already used, not just the position
Because gold values may be zero
items.answer: With four-direction movement and no revisits, the value depends on the whole set of cells already used, not just the position
items.explanation_md: A DP state must summarise the past compactly. For routes that can turn back around, the set of used cells matters, so there is no small state, which is why exhaustive search with undo is used.

items.prompt_md: In the gold DFS, what does the value returned by `dfs(r, c)` represent?
options: The number of cells visited so far
The best total gold collectable by a route that starts at (r, c) given the cells currently marked
The total gold in the whole grid
The best total over all starting cells
items.answer: The best total gold collectable by a route that starts at (r, c) given the cells currently marked
items.explanation_md: The call returns the cell's gold plus the best child result among unmarked neighbours. The max over all starts happens in the outer loop.

items.prompt_md: For the gold problem, what bounds the number of choices per step after the first one?
options: At most 3, because one of the four neighbours is the cell we just came from and it is marked
items.answer: At most 3, because one of the four neighbours is the cell we just came from and it is marked
items.explanation_md: The cell we arrived from is already marked, leaving at most 3 open neighbours, so a route of length L explores up to 3^L continuations.

items.prompt_md: What is the worst-case time of the gold DFS where L is the longest possible route length and there are `cells` cells?
items.answer: O(cells * 3^L)
items.explanation_md: Each cell is a starting point, and from each the search tree has branching of up to 3 and depth up to L. The result is exponential in L, which is why constraints keep the grid small.

items.prompt_md: What is the extra space of the in-place marking approach for a route of at most L cells?
options: O(L) for the recursion stack, with no separate visited structure
items.answer: O(L) for the recursion stack, with no separate visited structure
items.explanation_md: The marks live in the input grid, but each cell on the current route has an active stack frame, so recursion depth L is the space cost.

items.prompt_md: A teammate copies the visited set at every recursive call instead of marking in place. What is the cost?
options: O(L) extra work per step, since each copy is proportional to the route length
items.answer: O(L) extra work per step, since each copy is proportional to the route length
items.explanation_md: The copy preserves correctness but wastes time and memory per call. In-place mark and restore achieves the same effect in O(1).

items.prompt_md: Collect the largest total from a small grid of coins: start at any non-empty cell, move in four directions, and do not step on the same cell twice on one route.
options: DFS flood fill where cells stay visited
BFS with a queue for the fewest steps
items.answer: Grid backtracking: mark, explore, unmark
items.explanation_md: Each route needs its own used-set that is undone afterwards, because the best route may share cells with other tried routes. Flood fill, BFS and a position-only DP do not model that.

items.prompt_md: Count how many different walks cover every empty square of a small grid exactly once, from a given start to a given end.
options: DFS flood fill where cells stay visited
BFS with a queue for the fewest steps
items.answer: Grid backtracking: mark, explore, unmark
items.explanation_md: Counting every full walk is exhaustive search with mark and unmark. Flood fill would count cells, not walks.

items.prompt_md: Does a word appear in a letter grid when spelled by stepping to adjacent cells, never reusing a cell within the word?
options: DFS flood fill where cells stay visited
BFS with a queue for the fewest steps
items.answer: Grid backtracking: mark, explore, unmark
items.explanation_md: Each attempt at spelling the word is a route that must not reuse cells, and the cells must be freed for the next attempt. That is mark, explore, unmark.

items.prompt_md: Count the connected groups of land cells in a grid.
options: DFS flood fill where cells stay visited
items.answer: DFS flood fill where cells stay visited
items.explanation_md: Each cell needs to be visited once overall, so it stays marked. Unmarking would only add pointless work.

items.prompt_md: Find the fewest steps to walk from one corner of a grid with walls to the opposite corner.
options: DFS flood fill where cells stay visited
BFS with a queue for the fewest steps
items.answer: BFS with a queue for the fewest steps
items.explanation_md: A minimum number of uniform steps is the signature of BFS. Backtracking would try every route to find the minimum.

items.prompt_md: Count the number of ways to travel from the top-left to the bottom-right of a grid moving only right or down.
options: BFS with a queue for the fewest steps
DFS flood fill where cells stay visited
items.answer: Dynamic programming over (row, col)
items.explanation_md: The state is just the cell, so counts add from the cell above and left. Enumerating routes with backtracking would be exponential for no reason.

items.prompt_md: List every subset of a small set of numbers.
options: DFS flood fill where cells stay visited
items.answer: Subsets: include-or-skip recursion
items.explanation_md: Every element is either included or excluded, which is the subsets decision tree. There is no grid and no route.

items.prompt_md: List every ordering of a small set of distinct letters.
options: BFS with a queue for the fewest steps
items.answer: Permutations with a used-set
items.explanation_md: The order matters and each letter is used exactly once, so permutations with a used-set. Grid backtracking is the same mark-and-undo idea but is about movement in a grid.

items.prompt_md: Place non-attacking rooks on a chessboard so that no two share a row or column, and list all placements.
options: DFS flood fill where cells stay visited
Place one item per slot with conflict sets and pruning
items.answer: Place one item per slot with conflict sets and pruning
items.explanation_md: One item per row with column conflicts checked in O(1) is constraint placement, where the pruning comes from conflict sets.

items.prompt_md: A trail crosses a small grid, and you must find the longest simple trail (no cell repeated) from a fixed start.
options: BFS with a queue for the fewest steps
DFS flood fill where cells stay visited
items.answer: Grid backtracking: mark, explore, unmark
items.explanation_md: Longest simple trail means exhaustive search with undo. BFS finds shortest, and DP cannot summarise which cells are already on the trail.
